e.t: Abisou is a personal name, rendered “Abisou” or “Avisu.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in genealogical material, but its precise identification depends on the surrounding names and passage. It should therefore be read as a person’s name, with the spelling preserved according to the chosen rendering.

The word means “abyss”: a deep, unfathomable place or depth. As a noun, it refers to depths that lie beyond ordinary human reach or measurement. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 44 times, including passages connected with the deep waters, the earth’s depths, and places hidden from human sight. Its central idea is profound depth—something vast, inaccessible, and beyond ordinary limits. The precise force in any verse depends on how the surrounding passage describes that depth.

This word means “holy”: set apart for God, sacred, or belonging to what is devoted to him. As an adjective, it describes people, places, objects, times, and things marked as sacred; as a noun, it can refer to holy persons or sacred things. It is common throughout the Greek Old Testament and related books, occurring 594 times, with especially frequent use in Leviticus, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, and Psalms. Its central idea remains holiness and consecration.

This noun refers to “ill-repute” or “disgrace”: a state in which a person’s name or standing is held in dishonor. It describes damaged public regard rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, at Sirach 3:11. The word’s basic meaning is therefore a condition of dishonor; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that condition is presented there.

This LXX noun means “guilelessness”: a state of being free from deceit or crafty intent. It describes straightforward innocence rather than hidden schemes, and can characterize a person’s inner quality or conduct. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing in Job and Psalms. Its basic sense remains focused on sincerity and freedom from guile, while the precise emphasis in any verse depends on its surrounding wording.

This noun describes “licentiousness” or “intemperance”: conduct marked by a lack of restraint and self-control. It points to behavior that is not properly held in check, rather than merely an isolated mistake. The word appears once in the Greek LXX collection, in 4 Maccabees 13:7. Since the verse text is not provided here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context.

This noun means “upper city,” referring to the elevated or fortified part of a city. It names a place rather than an action, person, or quality. In this Greek biblical corpus, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its meaning remains consistent as a geographical term. The surrounding verse determines which city is meant in each occurrence, but the word itself points to the city’s higher district or stronghold.

Amethyst is the name of a precious stone. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun identifies the gemstone itself rather than an action, quality, or person. It occurs three times, in Exodus 28:19, Exodus 36:19, and Ezekiel 28:13. These occurrences place the word among descriptions of valuable or beautiful stones, while its basic meaning remains the name of the gem. The word’s precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the stone’s setting or use.

This verb means “carry up”: to move or bring something upward. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its exact sense in any particular sentence depends on what is being carried and where it is being brought, but the central idea remains upward movement or conveyance. [p03:word:lxx:L700977:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700977:occurrences]

This adjective means “husbandless,” describing a woman who does not have a husband. It identifies a marital condition rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 4 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains clear: lacking a husband. It is not a general term for being alone; it specifically concerns a woman’s marital status.

This word means “manly,” describing the manner in which an action is carried out. As an adverb, it tells the reader that someone acts in a manly way rather than naming a person or object. Its meaning is concise and direct, so it should not automatically be expanded into a specific virtue, emotion, or kind of courage without the surrounding verse. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees.

This Greek LXX adjective means “useless”: something that provides no benefit or helpful result. It describes a person, thing, or action as lacking practical value rather than merely being difficult or unpleasant. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this corpus, including Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any one verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as ineffective or unhelpful.

This adjective means “born,” describing someone as having come from or descended from a parent or family line. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings preserved in the LXX corpus, where it identifies a person by birth or descent rather than describing an action. The word occurs five times in five verses across 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “faint”: to lose strength or become unable to continue normally. It describes the act or state of fainting rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:18. The word’s basic sense is therefore clear, while the precise force of that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, not on the word alone.

This verb means “dishonor”: to treat a person as lacking the honor or regard due to them. It describes an action directed toward someone, rather than merely an inner feeling or opinion. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 33 times, showing repeated use for acts that lower, slight, or withhold proper honor from another person. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This adverb means “randomly” or “accidentally,” describing something done without a deliberate plan or fixed direction. It can express an action that happens by chance rather than through careful purpose. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:2. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense remains an action or event occurring unexpectedly or without intentional arrangement.

“Apharsachaioi; Afarsakhei” is a proper name used to identify a particular named group or people. It is not presented as an ordinary descriptive word with a general meaning, but as a designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezra: Ezra 5:6 and Ezra 6:6. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific identity and role of those named cannot be explained further here.

Achiezeri is a proper name, appearing in English as “Achiezeri” or “Akhiezeri.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:34. Because it is a name and no broader definition is supplied, its central meaning is the identification of the named person or entity associated with that occurrence. The exact role it carries in Numbers 26:34 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Achimi, also rendered Akhimi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament, and its role is simply to name that person. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 4:2. Without the verse text and surrounding genealogy, Scripture does not provide enough context here to say more about the person’s identity or significance.

Baalgad is a proper name, rendered as “Baalgad” or “Vaalgath.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Joshua, at Joshua 11:17 and Joshua 12:7. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in each passage cannot be described further, but its lexical meaning is the name itself.

Banaiou, also rendered Vaneu, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) text. The name occurs ten times across ten verses, including several passages in 1 Kings and additional occurrences in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel. Its significance in any particular passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding verse, not from a separate dictionary meaning attached to the name.

Basellan, also rendered Vasellan, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 21:30. Its precise identification and role depend on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This noun means “clod of earth,” referring to a lump or piece of soil. It names earth gathered into a distinct mass rather than loose dust or an abstract idea of land. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 7:5. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a physical clod of earth.

This Greek LXX verb means “marry”: to enter into marriage. It describes the act of marrying rather than naming a spouse, wedding, or marriage as a thing. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context, but its basic meaning remains the act of marrying. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament occurrence.

This word is the proper name “Damaskos; Thamaskos,” used to identify a named location rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 44 times, including passages from Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Amos. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points readers to the same named place whenever it occurs in the LXX.

Dessaos, also rendered “Thessaos,” is a proper name identifying a person. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; its meaning is tied to the individual who bears the name. This Greek LXX name occurs once, in the deuterocanonical book of 2 Maccabees, at 14:16. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the person’s role cannot be explained further here, but the lexical function is clear: it serves as a personal designation rather than a common noun or descriptive title.

This Greek LXX verb means “support.” It describes the action of supporting someone or something, rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across several books from Genesis through Proverbs. Its precise expression depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of support. The English rendering is not available here, so the clearest meaning is the stated sense “support.”

This noun refers to an assayer or scrutineer—someone who examines or tests carefully. It describes a person whose role is to inspect something closely and determine its quality or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Jeremiah 6:27. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central sense remains a careful examiner or tester.

This Greek LXX noun means “reception”: the receiving of people or an occasion arranged to receive them. It names a reception rather than the person who receives or the act of speaking. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing in Genesis and Esther. Its precise emphasis—whether the reception itself or the gathering connected with it—depends on the surrounding verse and its description.

This Greek LXX verb means “lie in; wrapped up in.” It describes something being situated within or enclosed in something else, rather than standing apart from it. As a verb, it expresses a condition or position: something lies in a place or is wrapped up in it. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, in Genesis and Esther. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being described and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “go.” It describes movement from one place toward another or progression onward. In the LXX corpus, it appears 4,430 times, making it a common word whose exact force is normally clarified by the sentence around it. Its central idea remains going or proceeding, whether referring to a person’s movement, a journey, or progress toward a destination. It is found throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented in this corpus.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Eleutheros” or “Eleftheros.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times across 18 verses. The exact person it identifies must be determined from the surrounding passage, since a name by itself does not describe that person’s role or significance.

Ememaon is a proper name preserved as “Ememaōn” or “Ememaon,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:28. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its underlying meaning. Its precise significance in Joshua therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.h: To Think or Keep in Mind
e.t: This verb means to have something in one’s thoughts—to think about it or keep it in mind. In the Greek Old Testament translation and related Greek writings, it describes inward mental attention rather than an outward action. The word occurs seven times in this corpus, appearing in both Old Testament books and later Greek Jewish writings. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This LXX Greek verb means “exalt”: to raise someone or something to a high position of honor or importance. It describes an action rather than a person, expressing the act of lifting up or honoring. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Daniel and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

This Greek word means “beg”: to ask someone earnestly for help, provision, or something needed. It is a verb, so it describes the act of making such a request rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice—once in Psalms and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a direct appeal for what one lacks or desires.

This noun means “interrogation”: a deliberate process of questioning someone to obtain information or an explanation. It refers to more than a casual question, emphasizing directed inquiry. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 43:7. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of questioning or being questioned in a formal, purposeful way.

This word means “fit,” describing something appropriate or well-suited for its intended use. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, thing, or circumstance as matching what is needed rather than being unsuitable. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalms 31:6. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is suitability or proper matching.

This adjective describes something of good size—something very large. It points to notable physical magnitude rather than naming an action or feeling. In the Greek LXX, it appears twice, once in 1 Samuel and once in Baruch, so it is an uncommon word in this corpus. Its basic sense remains straightforward: the person or thing described is impressively large or substantial. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself emphasizes size.

“Ephraim” is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings. It identifies a named biblical entity, while the surrounding passage determines whether the reference concerns a person, a tribe, or another use of the name. The word occurs 197 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Sirach. Its standard English rendering is “Ephraim,” with “Efrem” also given as a gloss.

This adverb means “thereupon” or “immediately afterwards,” marking an action or event that follows another in sequence. It draws attention to what happens next, without by itself explaining the reason for that next event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary meaning is a close temporal connection between two events.

This noun refers to the act of taking someone alive—capturing a person while they remain living. In the Greek Old Testament, or Septuagint, it occurs twice: in Numbers 21:35 and Deuteronomy 2:34. Its central idea is capture that preserves life, rather than describing death or destruction. These references show where the word appears, while the particular force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to the number nine. It functions as an indeclinable number, meaning its form does not change for grammatical purposes. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalm 118:65. The supplied lexical definition identifies it simply as “9; teth,” so its meaning is numerical rather than a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This adverb describes something done “wonderfully” or “terribly,” emphasizing that it is extraordinary in either a marvelous or fearsome way. It modifies an action or description rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs four times, across Psalms, Daniel, and Sirach. The exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea is that something is strikingly beyond the ordinary.

This noun means “censer,” a vessel used in worship for carrying or burning incense. It names a ritual utensil rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 24 times across 23 verses, appearing especially often in Numbers and also in Exodus, Kings, Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees. Its repeated use in descriptions of sacred furnishings and offerings shows that it refers to a recognizable implement used in the service of worship.

This noun refers to “hymns of praise”—songs or composed words directed toward honoring and celebrating God. It names praise expressed in a musical or poetic form rather than simply describing a feeling of admiration. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs once, at Nehemiah 12:27. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular role there, but its basic meaning is a designated expression of praise through hymns.

This is the personal name Jacob, rendered in Greek as “Iakōb” or “Iakov.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 396 times, with its greatest concentration in Genesis, where Jacob is first named. The name also appears throughout later biblical books when referring to him or to his descendants. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “ibis,” the name of a bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Isaiah 34:11. The word identifies the creature itself rather than an action, quality, or relationship. Because the available information does not include the verse’s wording or surrounding context, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained here. Its basic meaning remains simple and definite: an ibis, a particular kind of bird.

gl: Egyptian and Jewish liquid measure; hin
d: Egyptian and Jewish liquid measure; hin

e.t: This word refers to an Egyptian and Jewish liquid measure called a “hin.” It is a noun used for measuring liquids in Old Testament passages translated in the Greek Septuagint, especially in instructions concerning offerings, anointing oil, and other prescribed quantities. The word occurs 21 times across 18 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus, from Exodus through Ezekiel. Its meaning is a recognized measure of liquid rather than a description of the liquid itself.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Isphan” or “Isfan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:22. The available lexical information gives the name’s form and recognized renderings, but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and the person’s place within the genealogy.

This proper name identifies Joseph, written in the lexical gloss as “Iōsēph; Iosif.” It functions as a personal name rather than a common description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 226 times, with most occurrences in Genesis, where Joseph is a recurring named figure. The name continues to identify him in later biblical references. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “also I” or “and that”. It is a conjunction, so it joins one thought to another by adding a person, thing, or statement. In ordinary reading, it can mark inclusion—something or someone is added—and can also connect a further point. This Greek LXX word appears once, in 2 Maccabees 1:15. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to link and add rather than describe an action or object.

This verb means to bend—to curve, lower, or turn something from a straight or upright position. It can describe a physical movement or action, depending on the sentence around it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, showing that it is used across several settings rather than being limited to one passage. Its precise force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “cut in pieces” or “cut up.” It describes the act of dividing or slashing something into pieces, rather than merely making a small cut. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in four different verses. Its occurrences are found in Leviticus, 1 Kings, Isaiah, and Hosea, showing that the word can describe this severe physical action in several settings. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context.

“Hollowly” describes an action or statement done in an empty, insubstantial, or inwardly unproductive way. As an adverb, this word tells how something is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Isaiah 49:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its central idea is emptiness or lack of substantial result.

This noun refers to motion or movement—the act or process of something moving. It describes movement in a general sense rather than naming a person, object, or destination. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Maccabees 13:44 and 4 Maccabees 1:35. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine what kind of movement is intended in either passage, but the word’s basic meaning remains motion or movement.

This verb means “provide the ceiling with,” describing the act of furnishing or covering a ceiling as part of building work. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 6, a chapter describing construction details for the temple. Its wording points to an action performed on the ceiling rather than naming the ceiling itself. The exact object or material supplied is determined by the surrounding verse, but the basic sense is the work of equipping a ceiling.

This LXX noun means “punishment”—the penalty or corrective consequence associated with wrongdoing. It names what a person receives because of a guilty act, rather than describing the act itself. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including several passages in Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains punishment imposed in response to wrongdoing.

This Greek LXX noun means “stamp,” referring to a stamp or the mark associated with one. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 15:6. The word’s basic sense is limited and concrete: it identifies a stamp rather than describing an action, person, or quality. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but “stamp” is the supported meaning.

Lemna is a proper name, referring to a named individual or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Joshua and once in 2 Kings. Its meaning is simply the name “Lemna”; the available information does not establish a further word-picture or descriptive sense. Its exact referent in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Magebōs, also rendered Mayevos, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person, family, or group in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Ezra 2:30. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be identified more precisely here, but its basic function is clear: it serves as a personal or family name in that passage.

Makellath is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here with an expanded definition or descriptive meaning; its function is to identify something by name. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Numbers 33, and the English rendering remains “Makellath” in each occurrence. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

Mapsar is a proper name rendered “Mapsar,” not a common word describing an idea, action, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 24:7. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise referent therefore depends on the verse and surrounding passage, rather than on a broader lexical meaning.

Melcha, also rendered Melkha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs 11 times across 10 verses in the LXX, appearing from Genesis through Joshua. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is chiefly identification: it tells the reader which individual is being mentioned, while the surrounding passage supplies the person’s particular role or family connection.

This is a proper name rendered “Mēdōn” or “Mithon.” It functions as a name for a named entity in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, from 2 Kings through 1 Maccabees. Its precise identification in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This noun means “toil”: demanding, effortful work that requires sustained labor. It can describe the burden of working hard rather than a particular occupation or task. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 23 times, showing that the word is used across several books for the general experience of labor and exertion. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

Nadab, also rendered Nathav, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or general idea. The name occurs 20 times across 20 verses in this LXX corpus, from Exodus through Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the person named and the surrounding verse, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This noun means “guardian of the laws”—a person responsible for protecting, preserving, or upholding the laws. It describes an official or appointed keeper whose role is connected specifically with the law rather than with general security or protection. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:32. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is a person entrusted with guarding the laws.

This Greek LXX verb means “suppose”: to form an opinion, make an assumption, or consider something likely. It describes an act of thought rather than a physical action. The word appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing that it can be used whenever someone expresses a judgment or expectation. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what the speaker is considering.

This verb means “augur; learn by divination.” It describes seeking knowledge through divination rather than ordinary observation or instruction. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Deuteronomy 18:10, so its meaning is presented in a single occurrence within this corpus. The word names the practice itself: attempting to gain information or guidance through divination. Its precise force in Deuteronomy 18:10 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which provide the immediate context.

This word means “bread,” referring to ordinary food made from grain and used for nourishment. It is a noun, so it names the food itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 19:6. The reference identifies its sole recorded occurrence in this corpus, but without the verse text, its broader significance in that scene should not be inferred from the word alone. Its basic lexical meaning remains bread.

This word means “no one” or “not one.” It is used as a pronoun or adjective to exclude every person or indicate that not even one is present, involved, or included. Its precise application depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central force is clear: zero individuals or none of a group. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 246 times, so it is a broadly used way to express complete absence or exclusion.

This Greek LXX noun means “covering,” referring generally to something that covers or conceals. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation tradition, in Sirach 33:6. The word’s basic sense is clear, but its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its immediate context. It should therefore be understood as the name of a covering rather than as a broad theological idea or a description of a particular object beyond what the word itself states.

This noun means “party,” referring to a gathering or festive assembly. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs four times across four verses. Its basic sense identifies a communal celebration or public gathering rather than an individual person or private action. The surrounding passage determines whether the party is being mentioned as a joyful observance, a scheduled gathering, or something rejected in worship. This word appears in Ezekiel, Hosea, and Amos.

gl: eating of strange meat; indiscriminate eating
d: eating of strange meat; indiscriminate eating

e.t: This noun refers to eating strange meat—that is, indiscriminate eating without careful distinction about what is eaten. It names the practice itself, rather than a person who eats or an instruction to eat. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 1:27. That reference identifies where the word appears, while its lexical sense remains the act of eating strange or varied meat indiscriminately. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This verb means to “spend amiss” or “waste,” describing the misuse or squandering of something rather than its proper use. It presents waste as an action, so it can describe what someone does with resources, time, or another provision. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Numbers 17:27, but the available wording does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the particular situation there. Its central sense remains spending or using something wastefully.

This Greek LXX verb means to address someone or exhort them. It describes speaking directly to a person with an urging or appeal, rather than merely mentioning them. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 12:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is direct speech intended to encourage, urge, or call upon someone.

This noun means “trial”—a circumstance or experience that tests someone. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it appears 14 times, showing that it names a recurring kind of testing rather than a personal name or action word. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a trial or test. The word occurs across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings in this Greek corpus.

This adjective means “more” or “majority,” describing something greater in amount, number, or extent than something else. It can identify the larger portion or a greater number of people or things. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 75 times, so it is a commonly used term for comparison and quantity. Its exact sense in a particular sentence depends on what is being compared, but its central idea remains an increase, a greater share, or the larger group.

This verb means “enrich” or “be/get rich.” It describes gaining wealth or becoming prosperous, whether through increase in possessions or a changed financial condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 11 times, including passages rendered with ideas such as being rich or becoming enriched. Its use can therefore describe either making someone wealthy or coming to possess greater wealth. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended in a particular occurrence.

The word means “in fit manner; meetly”: it describes an action carried out suitably, appropriately, or in a way that properly fits the situation. As an adverb, it modifies an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality; it tells how something is done. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:12. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic idea is fitting or proper action.

This verb means “die also,” expressing that someone dies in addition to another person or group already mentioned. It is a verb describing death, with “also” connecting the death to another related death or circumstance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 21:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but its basic meaning is the added or shared experience of dying.

This word means “offering”: something presented or given, especially in a religious setting. It is a noun naming the gift or presentation itself rather than the act of offering. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, showing a recurring term for what is brought or presented. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains an offering given or presented.

This verb means “happen to be before” or “previously”; it refers to something that existed or occurred earlier than another thing. As a verb, it describes prior existence or precedence rather than an action taking place at the present moment. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Job 42:17. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is that something was already present or had happened beforehand.

This Greek LXX verb means “spit”: to expel saliva from the mouth. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Numbers and once in Sirach, showing the same straightforward bodily meaning in both places. The precise force of the action in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

Rēpha, also rendered “Rhifa,” is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:12. The available wording establishes the name itself, but without the verse text it does not provide further information about the person or the role this name has in that passage.

Salamanasar is a proper name referring to a person named Salamanasar. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 2 Kings 17:3. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes this individual from other people in the account. The name itself does not express a quality, action, or spiritual principle; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the person’s role there.

Semeron is a proper name, preserved in English as “Semeron,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, while the person or place it identifies must be determined from the surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Kings 16:24 and once in 1 Chronicles 7:1. Sephei (also rendered “Sefi”) is a proper name—the personal name of an individual, rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:37. The available lexical information identifies it by these name forms but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. This noun means “contemptuous behaviour”: conduct that shows scorn, disrespect, or disdain toward someone. It describes an outward manner rather than merely an inward feeling, identifying actions or behavior that treat another person as unworthy of respect. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, in Sirach 41:21. Its precise force in that passage is understood from the surrounding verse and wider context.

This Greek LXX verb means “look angry,” describing an outward expression that appears stern, displeased, or wrathful. It functions as an action word, telling how someone presents their face or appearance rather than naming anger as an inner feeling. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, across Psalms, Proverbs, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains the visible appearance of anger.

“Emery powder” is a noun naming a powder material. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 41:7. The available lexical meaning identifies the material itself, but the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, so its precise role in that passage cannot be described safely. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: it refers to emery powder rather than to a person, action, or quality.

The word means “chain,” naming an object made of connected links. It is a noun, so it identifies the thing itself rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Judges 8:26. Its basic meaning is therefore clear, while its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text. The singular lexical idea may be rendered in English according to the sentence’s number and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “general” and refers to serving or acting in the role of a general. Because it is a verb, it describes what someone does rather than naming the commander himself. In the LXX evidence available here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. The exact force in either verse depends on its surrounding passage, but its basic idea concerns generalship and military command.

This verb means “mix in with” or “mingle,” describing the act of becoming joined or intermingled with others. It presents mixing as an action rather than naming a person, object, or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 23:12. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word’s basic sense is to enter into mixture or close association with something else.

In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Deuteronomy and once in Wisdom. The word therefore presents fighting as assistance given for someone else, with the helper joining the struggle on that person’s side.

This verb means “pull down” or “pull about,” describing an action of dragging or forcefully drawing something around. It is a Greek LXX word found once in the supplied corpus, in 2 Maccabees 5:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the precise object and force of the action must be determined from that passage. Its basic sense remains an active movement of pulling something down or about.

This Greek LXX word means “quick,” describing something that happens or moves with speed. As an adjective, it can describe a person or thing as quick; as an adverb, it can describe an action done quickly. It appears 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, including Proverbs, Jeremiah, Nahum, and Zephaniah. Its exact force in any verse depends on what it modifies and the surrounding sentence.

This noun means “kingly power” or “sovereignty”: the authority, dominion, or ruling power associated with a king or ruler. It names the possession or exercise of royal authority rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs seven times, including in Esther, Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

Pheleththi, also rendered Feleththi, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs six times in this LXX corpus, appearing in 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of its personal meaning.

This adjective describes someone who is quarrelsome—inclined to argue, dispute, or create conflict. It portrays a contentious disposition rather than simply identifying a single disagreement. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Ezekiel 3:7, so its precise force there belongs to that passage’s surrounding context. Its basic sense remains clear: a person characterized by strife or a readiness to quarrel.

Chabra, also rendered Khavra, is a proper name identifying a place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:40. Because the name is preserved as a place-name and no further definition is given, its meaning is best expressed by identifying the named location rather than assigning it an unrelated Hebrew or Greek idea. This adjective means “bright,” describing something marked by brightness or a shining appearance. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Genesis 49:12. The word’s basic sense is straightforward: it identifies a visible quality rather than an action, person, or relationship. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains brightness. As an adjective, it describes a noun by attributing this quality to it.

“Need be” expresses necessity: something is required or must be so. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb appears once, at Proverbs 32:27, so its lexical range is represented by a single occurrence. It states that an action or condition is necessary rather than merely possible or preferred. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains necessity. This is a Greek LXX word and remains distinct from Hebrew and Greek New Testament source-word entries.

This word means to sing psalms, expressing praise through song. It is a verb describing the act of singing, especially in worship or praise directed to God. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, with most occurrences in the Psalms. The related wording can also describe a woman who sings, but its central sense remains singing psalms rather than merely speaking or making music in general.
